subtitulo: Seven days the whole country is off, two nights that take over the street, and one week that is not an official holiday and still closes half of everything
cena: You booked the museum for Monday, and the person at the desk has just made the face of somebody about to explain a bridge.
frasePiso: Two questions before you book anything — is it a holiday, and are you closing — buy you the whole calendar without memorising a single date.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Mexican federal labour law establishes a small set of obligatory rest days (días de asueto), including 1 January, the first Monday of February, the third Monday of March, 1 May, 16 September, the third Monday of November and 25 December — several deliberately moved to Monday to create a long weekend.
fatosDatados.fonte: Ley Federal del Trabajo, artigo 74; calendários oficiais de feriados de 2026

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Several of the most observed dates are not obligatory rest days: Día de Muertos runs 31 October to 2 November (with 2 November commonly closed), 12 December is the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe, and Semana Santa is not an official holiday yet is one of the heaviest travel weeks of the year, with many businesses on reduced hours.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes sobre feriados mexicanos (Mexperience — «Guide to Public & Civic Holidays in Mexico»; Britannica; calendários de 2026)

steps.pt: You will not memorise the Mexican calendar. You will learn two questions that make the calendar tell you itself.
You planned the museum for Monday. The person at the desk is making the face of somebody about to explain a puente.

steps.es: El lunes hacen puente, joven. Cerramos.
steps.pt: Monday's a long weekend — we're closed.
steps.tts: El lunes hacen puente, joven. Cerramos.

steps.pt: A puente is a holiday moved to Monday so the weekend stretches. Several of the seven national rest days work that way.

steps.promptPt: Before you commit to any plan, ask the direct question. Speak now.

steps.es: Sí, y el martes muchos no abren tampoco.
steps.pt: Yes, and a lot of places don't open Tuesday either.
steps.tts: Sí, y el martes muchos no abren tampoco.

steps.pt: That second half only comes if you ask the follow-up. Official closing and actual closing are different lists.

steps.promptPt: Ask about this place specifically, not about the country. Speak now.
steps.pt: Are you going to be open?
Now the dates that close things unofficially: Día de Muertos, the 31st to the 2nd. Guadalupe on 12 December. And Semana Santa.
Semana Santa is not a legal holiday and it empties offices and fills every beach. Plan around it or plan into it.

steps.es: En Semana Santa no encuentras nada, todo se llena.
steps.pt: 👂 Not a warning about danger — a warning about capacity. Book early or go elsewhere.
steps.tts: En Semana Santa no encuentras nada, todo se llena.

steps.promptPt: A holiday is coming and you'd rather be in it than avoid it. Ask what actually happens. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: keh seh AH-seh ah-KEE EH-seh DEE-ah
steps.pt: What do people do here that day?

steps.es: Se pone el altar y vamos al panteón en la noche.
steps.pt: We set up the altar and go to the cemetery at night.
steps.tts: Se pone el altar y vamos al panteón en la noche.

steps.pt: That is an answer about a family, not a festival — so the next question decides if you're a spectator or a guest.

steps.promptPt: Ask whether it's alright for a visitor to go, rather than assuming either way. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Está bien si va uno de fuera?
steps.pinyin: ehs-TAH byen see bah OO-noh deh FWEH-rah
steps.pt: Is it alright for an outsider to go?
steps.tts: ¿Está bien si va uno de fuera?

steps.promptPt: Get the practical detail you'll actually need: what time it starts. Speak now.

steps.es: ¿El lunes es día festivo? ¿Ustedes van a abrir? ¿Qué se hace aquí ese día?
steps.pinyin: el LOO-nehs ehs DEE-ah fehs-TEE-boh. oos-TEH-dehs bahn ah ah-BREER. keh seh AH-seh ah-KEE EH-seh DEE-ah
steps.pt: Shadow the two planning questions and the one that gets you invited.
steps.tts: ¿El lunes es día festivo? ¿Ustedes van a abrir? ¿Qué se hace aquí ese día?

steps.pt: A06 complete. Ask if it is a holiday, then ask if they are opening. And ask what people do — that turns a closed day around.

secoes.corpo: Federal labour law sets a short list of obligatory días de asueto, and several are deliberately shifted to Monday to create the puente. That list is what banks and government offices follow.

Día de Muertos, 12 December for the Virgin of Guadalupe, and the days around Christmas close far more doors than the legal list would predict. A date can be unofficial and still shut the street you were going to.

secoes.titulo: Semana Santa is the big one
secoes.corpo: It is not a public holiday and it is the heaviest domestic travel week of the year. Beaches fill, intercity buses sell out, and city offices empty. Nothing about the legal calendar warns you.

secoes.titulo: Ask the place, not the country
secoes.corpo: ¿Es día festivo? gets you the national rule. ¿Ustedes van a abrir? gets you the answer you actually needed, because a small business decides for itself and often closes for dates that appear on no list at all.

permissao: You are allowed to plan around a holiday instead of through it. Deciding to skip a packed Semana Santa beach is not missing out — half the country makes exactly that calculation every year, and the ones who go accept the crowd on purpose.
espelho: Anyone who has watched a foreign visitor turn up expecting normal service on a national holiday at home knows this from the other side — the information was public, it just wasn't in the guidebook they were carrying. The fix is the same in both directions: ask a local before you book.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You check that a date isn't on the official public holiday list, plan around it, and still find the place closed and the buses full.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: The information I found was wrong, or this place is unreliable.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Mexico has two calendars that don't overlap: the short legal list of obligatory rest days, and a much longer list of dates that are genuinely observed — Día de Muertos, 12 December, Semana Santa — which close businesses without appearing in labour law at all.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask a person rather than a list, and ask twice: is it a holiday, and are you specifically going to be open.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the real answer for the actual place you're going, which is the only answer that was ever going to help.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for large hotels, airports and chains aimed at travellers, which generally do run through holidays — the mismatch bites hardest with small businesses, museums and government offices.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Someone describes what their family does for Día de Muertos, and you're not sure whether asking to come along would be intrusive.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: It's about their dead relatives, so it must be private — a visitor asking would be tasteless.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Día de Muertos spans both registers at once: public celebration in plazas and streets, and a family observance at the cemetery. Which one you've been told about determines the answer, and the person telling you knows exactly which they meant.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask directly whether it's alright for an outsider to go, and take the answer at face value either way.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You either get invited into something you could never have bought a ticket for, or you get a clear no that costs nothing — and the question itself reads as respect rather than intrusion.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a licence to photograph a family at a graveside — being welcome somewhere and being welcome to document it are separate permissions, and the second one has to be asked for separately.
